title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence: the imitation game
text:
CHAPTER 8. TURING 1950 AND THE BIRTH OF AI
SECTION 8.1. COMPUTING MACHINERY AND INTELLIGENCE: THE IMITATION GAME

In October 1950 the philosophy journal Mind published a paper by Alan Turing that began: "I propose to consider the question, 'Can machines think?'" Turing immediately set the question aside as too vague and replaced it with a concrete test he called the imitation game, now known as the Turing test. The paper, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence," also answered nine objections to machine intelligence and sketched how a thinking machine might be built by teaching a "child machine." It remains the most cited founding document of artificial intelligence, and its predictions have recently been tested by large language models. This section reads the paper closely.

1. Context

By 1950 Turing had defined computation (1936; Chapter 3), worked on codebreaking (Section 3.3), designed the ACE computer (Section 4.4), and moved to the University of Manchester, where the Manchester Mark 1 and then the Ferranti Mark 1 were running. He had already written about machine intelligence in an unpublished 1948 report for the National Physical Laboratory, "Intelligent Machinery," which discussed learning machines and networks of simple neuron-like units it called "unorganized machines." (That report was not published until the late 1960s.) In it he observed that the extent to which we regard something as behaving intelligently depends as much on our own state of mind and training as on the properties of the object, which explains why he later chose a behavioral test.

2. The imitation game

Turing first described a party game with three players: a man (A), a woman (B) and an interrogator (C) of either sex, in a separate room. Communication is by typewritten messages so that voices do not give anything away. The interrogator's object is to determine which is the man and which the woman; A tries to mislead the interrogator, B tries to help.

Then he asked: "What will happen when a machine takes the part of A in this game?" Will the interrogator decide wrongly as often when the game is played with a machine as when it is played between a man and a woman? This question, Turing said, replaces "Can machines think?"

The paper's own framing has been read in slightly different ways, and later writers usually simplified it to the version most people know: an interrogator converses by text with a human and a machine and must decide which is which. If the interrogator cannot reliably tell, the machine passes.

Why this test? Turing gave several reasons:

  - It avoids the impossible task of defining "thinking" and "machine" precisely.
  - It separates intellectual capacity from physical appearance: "We do not wish to penalise the machine for its inability to shine in beauty competitions."
  - Conversation is open-ended. The interrogator can ask about anything: arithmetic, poetry, chess, emotions. Turing gave sample exchanges, including a request for a sonnet, a sum, and a chess problem.

He also specified what "machine" means: a digital computer. He explained digital computers for the Mind audience (store, executive unit, control, as in Section 4.4), and stressed that by the universality property (Section 3.2) a single digital computer, suitably programmed, can imitate any discrete-state machine. So the question becomes whether there are imaginable digital computers that would do well in the game.

3. The prediction

Turing made a specific technological prediction:

    "I believe that in about fifty years' time it will be possible to programme computers, with a storage capacity of about 10^9, to make them play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator will not have more than 70 per cent chance of making the right identification after five minutes of questioning."

Note the details. "Storage capacity of about 10^9" means about 10^9 binary digits, roughly 125 megabytes. A 70 percent chance of correct identification means the machine fools the interrogator at least 30 percent of the time, a modest bar. And only five minutes of questioning.

He also made a sociological prediction: that by the end of the century "the use of words and general educated opinion will have altered so much that one will be able to speak of machines thinking without expecting to be contradicted."

How did these fare? By 2000, personal computers had far more than 10^9 bits of storage, but no program came close to passing a serious version of the test. Turing underestimated the difficulty of the software, not the hardware. Language turned out to be among the hardest problems in AI (Chapters 9, 17-19).

4. The nine objections

Much of the paper responds to objections. They remain a useful map of the debates around AI.

  1. The theological objection: thinking is a function of the immortal soul, which God gave to humans but not machines. Turing replied that this restricts God's omnipotence and that in building such machines "we should not be irreverently usurping His power of creating souls, any more than we are in the procreation of children."

  2. The "heads in the sand" objection: the consequences of machines thinking would be too dreadful, so let us hope they cannot. Turing said this needs consolation more than refutation.

  3. The mathematical objection: Goedel's theorem and Turing's own results (Sections 1.2, 3.1) show that any given machine has questions it cannot answer. Turing replied that humans also make mistakes and cannot answer everything, and that there is no proof that humans are free of such limits. One machine may be limited, but it might be outdone only by another machine.

  4. The argument from consciousness: a machine cannot really feel or know it has written a sonnet. Turing argued that taken to the extreme this leads to solipsism: we only know other people think by their behavior, and it is a "polite convention" to assume that everyone thinks. If a machine could answer questions about a sonnet it wrote as a person might, most people would extend the same convention.

  5. Arguments from various disabilities: "a machine can never do X," where X is be kind, have a sense of humor, fall in love, enjoy strawberries and cream, learn from experience, be the subject of its own thought, and so on. Turing suggested these come from induction over the limited machines people had seen.

  6. Lady Lovelace's objection: the Analytical Engine "has no pretensions to originate anything" (Section 1.3). Turing replied that machines take him by surprise frequently, and that the objection would not apply to learning machines whose behavior is not fully foreseen by their programmers.

  7. The argument from continuity in the nervous system: the brain is not a discrete-state machine. Turing replied that a digital computer can imitate a continuous machine closely enough that an interrogator could not tell the difference.

  8. The argument from informality of behaviour: humans cannot be governed by a complete set of rules of conduct, so they are not machines. Turing distinguished rules of conduct from laws of behavior and argued we cannot be sure there are no laws governing us.

  9. The argument from extrasensory perception: Turing, reflecting a period in which some researchers took ESP experiments seriously, said the statistical evidence for telepathy was "overwhelming" and suggested a telepathy-proof room for the test. Modern readers generally view this section as a product of its time.

5. Learning machines and the child machine

The last section of the paper, "Learning Machines," is the most forward-looking. Turing estimated that programming a machine to play the imitation game by writing all the rules directly would require enormous effort, and he proposed instead:

    "Instead of trying to produce a programme to simulate the adult mind, why not rather try to produce one which simulates the child's? If this were then subjected to an appropriate course of education one would obtain the adult brain."

He divided the problem into designing a "child machine" and designing an education process, and compared it to evolution:

    structure of the child machine = hereditary material
    changes of the child machine   = mutation
    judgment of the experimenter   = natural selection

He discussed teaching with rewards and punishments ("pleasure" and "pain" signals), noting that a learning machine would need more than these to learn efficiently, and that the teacher would often be largely ignorant of what was going on inside the machine, "although he may still be able to some extent to predict his pupil's behaviour." He suggested that introducing randomness into a learning machine could be useful, for instance when searching for a solution among many possibilities.

Read today, this section describes in outline the program of machine learning: rather than programming intelligence, build a system that learns from experience, guided by reward (reinforcement learning, Section 16.4) and teaching (supervised learning), with internals that are partly opaque even to its designers (the interpretability problem of modern neural networks). Large language models are, loosely speaking, a realization of this idea: a general learning architecture trained on vast data, then "educated" with human feedback (Section 19.1).

Turing ended with: "We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done."

6. Criticisms of the test

The Turing test has been criticized on many grounds:

  - It tests deception and human-likeness rather than intelligence. A machine that is far smarter than humans but answers instantly or never makes typos would be detected easily.
  - It is anthropocentric. Animals and possibly machines could be intelligent in non-human ways.
  - It can be gamed. Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA (1966; Section 9.4) showed how simple pattern-matching tricks could make people attribute understanding to a program.
  - The Chinese Room. In 1980 the philosopher John Searle argued that a person following rules to manipulate Chinese symbols, without understanding Chinese, could produce correct answers; therefore passing a behavioral test does not show understanding. Responses to Searle (the systems reply, the robot reply and others) have been debated ever since.

Most AI researchers have not treated passing the Turing test as a research goal; they have worked on specific capabilities. But the test endures as a cultural benchmark.

7. Attempts at the test

  - The Loebner Prize, launched in 1990 by Hugh Loebner with the Cambridge Center for Behavioral Studies, held annual restricted Turing test competitions starting in November 1991. The programs were mostly chatbots with scripted tricks; the competition ended after its 2019 edition.
  - In 2014 a chatbot called Eugene Goostman, presented as a 13-year-old Ukrainian boy (an excuse for poor English and limited knowledge), was reported to have convinced 33 percent of judges in a five-minute test at an event organized by the University of Reading. Many researchers criticized the claim that this "passed" the test, because of the persona trick and the short format.
  - In 2025, researchers Cameron Jones and Benjamin Bergen of the University of California, San Diego, reported a randomized, controlled three-party Turing test (posted as a preprint in March 2025 titled "Large Language Models Pass the Turing Test"). When instructed to adopt a humanlike persona, GPT-4.5 was judged to be the human 73 percent of the time, more often than the actual human participants. The original ELIZA, included as a baseline, fared poorly.

So, measured by Turing's own five-minute criterion, his prediction came true about 75 years after the paper rather than 50, and on computers with vastly more than 10^9 bits of storage. Whether that means the machines "think" remains, as Turing anticipated, a matter of how "general educated opinion" uses the words.

8. Why the paper still matters

  - It made machine intelligence a respectable scientific question.
  - It framed intelligence behaviorally, an operational approach that runs through AI's later emphasis on benchmarks.
  - It anticipated, in a few pages, machine learning, reinforcement learning, evolutionary methods, and the opacity of learned systems.
  - Its list of objections still structures debates about AI consciousness, creativity and limits.

9. Summary

  - Turing's "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" (Mind, October 1950) replaced "Can machines think?" with the imitation game, a text-based test of whether an interrogator can distinguish machine from human.
  - He predicted that in about fifty years machines with about 10^9 bits of storage would leave an average interrogator no more than a 70 percent chance of correct identification after five minutes.
  - He answered nine objections, including Lady Lovelace's and the argument from consciousness.
  - He proposed building a "child machine" and educating it with rewards, punishments and teaching, an early sketch of machine learning.
  - Critics include Weizenbaum's ELIZA effect and Searle's Chinese Room (1980). The Loebner Prize (1991-2019) and Eugene Goostman (2014) were limited attempts; in a 2025 controlled study, GPT-4.5 with a persona prompt was judged human 73 percent of the time.
